question: Motion in a plane is best described as motion in which the position of a body changes with respect to:
explanation: Motion in a plane means that the body’s position cannot be fully described by a single coordinate alone. Two coordinates, usually along the \(x\)-axis and \(y\)-axis, are needed to locate the body at an instant. This is an extension of straight-line motion, where one coordinate may be enough. The path may be curved or slanting, but the description still uses two perpendicular directions. Time is needed to describe how the position changes, but time alone does not locate the body in space.

question: A stone is thrown obliquely upward from the ground. Its motion is usually treated as motion in a plane because:
opt_b: it has both horizontal and vertical components
opt_d: its acceleration must be along the horizontal direction
explanation: An obliquely thrown stone moves horizontally as well as vertically. A single straight-line coordinate cannot describe both changes at the same time. The horizontal part is naturally described along the \(x\)-axis, and the vertical part along the \(y\)-axis. This makes projectile motion a standard example of motion in a plane. The motion is not classified this way because of mass change or zero speed; it is classified by the need for two position coordinates.

question: A car moves only along a straight east-west road. Compared with an aircraft changing both altitude and horizontal position, the car’s motion:
opt_a: necessarily needs two coordinates, but the aircraft needs only one
opt_b: needs one coordinate, while the aircraft needs more than one.
opt_c: has no displacement because the road is straight
explanation: Motion along a fixed straight road can be described by one coordinate measured along that road. The car may move east or west, but it remains on the same line. An aircraft changing altitude and horizontal position cannot usually be located by one coordinate alone. It needs at least two coordinates when its motion is studied in a vertical plane. Straight-line motion is therefore a special simpler case, while plane motion needs a two-coordinate description.

question: In the description of motion in a plane, the pair \((x,y)\) gives:
opt_a: only the speed of the body
opt_c: only the observation time in the chosen frame
opt_d: the mass and acceleration values of the body
explanation: The ordered pair \((x,y)\) tells where the body is located relative to the chosen coordinate axes. The value \(x\) gives the position along the \(x\)-axis, while \(y\) gives the position along the \(y\)-axis. These two coordinates together locate a point in a plane. They do not directly give speed, mass, or acceleration. A coordinate pair is about position first; changes in position with time lead to velocity and acceleration.

question: The physical quantity \(\vec{r}\) used in plane motion most commonly represents:
explanation: The symbol \(\vec{r}\) is commonly used for the position vector of a body. It gives the position of the body with respect to a chosen origin. Since it is a vector, it includes both magnitude and direction from the origin to the point. In a plane, \(\vec{r}\) is usually described through its \(x\)- and \(y\)-coordinates. Path length is different because it depends on the route followed, while \(\vec{r}\) refers to location from the origin.

question:
Match the basic plane-motion quantities with their usual SI units.
QuantityUnit
P. Displacement1. \(\text{s}\)
Q. Time2. \(\text{m s}^{-2}\)
R. Velocity3. \(\text{m}\)
S. Acceleration4. \(\text{m s}^{-1}\)
The suitable matching is:
explanation: Displacement measures change in position, so its SI unit is \(\text{m}\). Time is measured in \(\text{s}\). Velocity is displacement per unit time, so its unit is \(\text{m s}^{-1}\). Acceleration is change in velocity per unit time, so its unit is \(\text{m s}^{-2}\). The powers of \(\text{s}\) help separate velocity from acceleration: one time factor appears in velocity, while two time factors appear in acceleration.

question: A river boat moves with respect to the water while the river current also carries it downstream. This situation is naturally treated as motion in a plane when:
opt_b: the boat is at rest relative to the river bank
opt_c: only the depth of the river is measured
opt_d: both along-river and across-river components are involved
explanation: A river-crossing situation may involve motion across the river and motion along the river due to current. These two directions are usually taken as perpendicular components in a plane. The actual motion seen from the bank is a combined effect of both directions. This makes a two-coordinate description useful. The mass of the boat is not what decides whether the motion is in a plane; the need for two directional components does.

question: The quantity \(\Delta\vec{r}\) in plane motion refers to:
explanation: The symbol \(\Delta\vec{r}\) means change in the position vector. It connects the initial and final positions of the body. Since it is a vector, it has both magnitude and direction. It is different from the total path length travelled, which may be longer for a curved path. The delta symbol \(\Delta\) signals change, and the arrow over \(\vec{r}\) signals vector character.

question: In a rectangular coordinate frame for plane motion, the origin \(O\) is used as:
opt_a: the point from which coordinates are measured
opt_b: the point where every moving body must remain
opt_c: the direction of velocity at every instant
explanation: The origin \(O\) is the reference point of the coordinate system. Coordinates such as \((x,y)\) are measured from this point along the chosen axes. A body need not stay at the origin; the origin is only a reference for locating it. Changing the origin can change coordinate values, even when the physical position of the body has not changed. This is why coordinates are always meaningful only after the reference frame has been chosen.

question: A point has coordinates \((-3\,\text{m}, 4\,\text{m})\) in a rectangular frame. This means the point lies:
explanation:
\( \textbf{Coordinate reading:} \) The first coordinate gives the \(x\)-position and the second coordinate gives the \(y\)-position.
\( \textbf{Given point:} \) \((-3\,\text{m},4\,\text{m})\).
\( \textbf{x-direction meaning:} \) The value \(-3\,\text{m}\) means \(3\,\text{m}\) on the negative side of the \(x\)-axis.
\( \textbf{y-direction meaning:} \) The value \(4\,\text{m}\) means \(4\,\text{m}\) on the positive side of the \(y\)-axis.
\( \textbf{Sign use:} \) The negative sign belongs only to the \(x\)-coordinate here.
\( \textbf{Position interpretation:} \) The point is left of the origin if positive \(x\) is taken to the right, and above the origin if positive \(y\) is upward.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The point lies \(3\,\text{m}\) along negative \(x\) and \(4\,\text{m}\) along positive \(y\).

question: A moving object is recorded at the same instant as \(x=5\,\text{m}\) and \(y=2\,\text{m}\). The phrase “same instant” is important because:
opt_a: both coordinates describe one position at the same time
opt_b: the body can have only \(x\)-motion and no \(y\)-motion
opt_c: time has the same unit as displacement
opt_d: the coordinates become independent of the chosen origin
explanation: In plane motion, the coordinates \(x\) and \(y\) together locate the body at a particular instant. If the two coordinates were taken at different times, they might not describe the same position of the moving body. The same time \(t\) is therefore used when describing both directions. This idea becomes especially important when equations of motion are later applied separately along \(x\) and \(y\). Separate coordinate directions do not mean separate clocks for the two parts of the motion.

question: A path is curved on a sheet of graph paper, and the position of a small bead is marked at different times. A two-dimensional description is needed mainly because:
opt_a: the bead has no velocity on a curved path
opt_b: both coordinates may change with time
opt_c: curved paths cannot be measured in metres
opt_d: acceleration is absent whenever a path is drawn on paper
explanation: A curved path in a plane usually cannot be described by only one coordinate. As the bead moves, its \(x\)-coordinate and \(y\)-coordinate may both change. The coordinate pair \((x,y)\) gives a complete location on the graph paper. The use of metres is still valid because position and displacement are lengths. Curvature does not remove velocity or acceleration; it only makes direction and coordinate description more important.

question:
Read the short record below.
At \(t=0\,\text{s}\), a toy car is at \((0\,\text{m},0\,\text{m})\). At \(t=2\,\text{s}\), it is at \((6\,\text{m},0\,\text{m})\). At \(t=4\,\text{s}\), it is at \((6\,\text{m},5\,\text{m})\).
What does the record show about the car’s motion?
opt_a: The car has moved only along one fixed coordinate direction during the whole record
opt_b: The car’s position changed first along \(x\) and later along \(y\)
opt_c: The car’s time coordinate changed but its position did not
opt_d: The car’s coordinates are meaningless because one value is zero
explanation: From \(t=0\,\text{s}\) to \(t=2\,\text{s}\), the \(x\)-coordinate changes from \(0\,\text{m}\) to \(6\,\text{m}\), while the \(y\)-coordinate remains \(0\,\text{m}\). From \(t=2\,\text{s}\) to \(t=4\,\text{s}\), the \(x\)-coordinate remains \(6\,\text{m}\), while the \(y\)-coordinate changes from \(0\,\text{m}\) to \(5\,\text{m}\). This record uses coordinate changes to describe motion in a plane. A zero coordinate is still meaningful because it tells that the point lies on an axis for that coordinate. The same object can have different coordinate changes during different parts of its motion.

question: The pair of axes used in elementary plane motion is usually chosen perpendicular to each other because:
opt_a: perpendicular axes make every path straight
opt_b: perpendicular axes remove the need for time
opt_c: perpendicular axes make acceleration equal to zero
opt_d: they allow independent readings along two axes
explanation: Rectangular coordinate axes are chosen perpendicular because they give a clean way to describe position in two independent directions. The \(x\)-coordinate is read along one axis, and the \(y\)-coordinate is read along the other. This does not force the actual path to be straight; the object may still move along a curved path. The choice of axes is a method of description, not a physical force acting on the object. Time is still needed to describe how the coordinates change during motion.

question: In a coordinate description of plane motion, changing the origin can change:
opt_c: the coordinate values assigned to the same point
opt_d: the fact that acceleration is measured in \(\text{m s}^{-2}\)
explanation: Coordinates are measured relative to a chosen origin. If the origin is shifted, the same physical point may receive different coordinate values. This does not mean the point itself has physically moved. The units of displacement, time, velocity, and acceleration are not changed by shifting the origin. Coordinate values are reference-dependent, while the physical event being described remains the same.

question: A body is at \((2\,\text{m},3\,\text{m})\) at one instant and later at \((2\,\text{m},7\,\text{m})\). The coordinate record most directly shows:
opt_a: no motion, because the \(x\)-coordinate is unchanged
opt_b: motion only along the \(y\)-direction during this interval
opt_c: motion only along the \(x\)-direction during this interval
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial position:} \) \((2\,\text{m},3\,\text{m})\).
\( \textbf{Final position:} \) \((2\,\text{m},7\,\text{m})\).
\( \textbf{x-coordinate change:} \) \(2\,\text{m}-2\,\text{m}=0\,\text{m}\), so there is no change along \(x\).
\( \textbf{y-coordinate change:} \) \(7\,\text{m}-3\,\text{m}=4\,\text{m}\), so there is a change along \(y\).
\( \textbf{Coordinate interpretation:} \) The position has changed even though one coordinate stayed constant.
\( \textbf{Direction reading:} \) The change is along the positive \(y\)-direction for this interval.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The record shows motion only along the \(y\)-direction during the interval.

question: Speed and velocity are both used to describe motion, but they differ because:
opt_a: speed has direction only, while velocity has magnitude only
opt_b: speed is always negative, while velocity is always positive
opt_c: speed is measured in \(\text{m}\), while velocity is measured in \(\text{s}\)
opt_d: speed has magnitude only, while velocity has magnitude and direction
explanation: Speed is a scalar quantity because it gives only how fast a body is moving. Velocity is a vector quantity because it gives both how fast the body is moving and in which direction it is moving. Both speed and velocity have the same SI unit, \(\text{m s}^{-1}\), so the difference is not in the unit. A negative sign attached to one component of velocity may indicate direction along a chosen axis, but speed itself is not a vector direction. The useful distinction is that speed can be found from distance per time, while velocity depends on displacement per time.

question: A quantity is classified as a vector only when it has:
opt_a: magnitude and unit but no direction
explanation: A vector quantity must have both magnitude and direction. Displacement, velocity, acceleration, and force are examples because their directions affect the physical description. A scalar quantity such as mass or time may have a magnitude and a unit, but it does not need a spatial direction. A sign alone is not enough to make a quantity a vector; the sign may only show positive or negative sense along a chosen line. Direction in space is the feature that separates a vector from a scalar.

question:
The table below lists some physical quantities.
RowQuantity groupClassification claimed
PMass, time, distanceScalars
QDisplacement, velocity, accelerationVectors
RSpeed, distance, timeVectors
SForce, displacement, velocityVectors
The row that does not fit the usual scalar-vector classification is:
explanation: Mass, time, and distance are scalar quantities because each has magnitude but no required direction. Displacement, velocity, acceleration, and force are vectors because direction is essential in describing them. Speed is a scalar because it only tells the rate of motion, not the direction of motion. Distance is also scalar because it measures the total path length without direction. Row R wrongly classifies speed, distance, and time as vectors, even though all three are scalars.

question: A runner completes one full round of a circular track and returns to the starting point. For the complete round, the distance covered and displacement are best described as:
opt_a: distance is zero, displacement is zero
opt_b: distance is non-zero, displacement is zero
opt_c: distance is zero, displacement is non-zero
opt_d: distance and displacement are both equal to the radius
explanation: Distance is the total length of the path actually travelled. In one complete round of a circular track, the runner has covered the circumference, so the distance is not zero. Displacement depends only on the initial and final positions. Since the runner returns to the starting point, the initial and final positions are the same. The displacement vector is therefore \(\vec{0}\), even though the runner has certainly travelled a non-zero path length.

question:
Assertion: A scalar quantity can be added algebraically without considering spatial direction.
Reason: A scalar quantity has magnitude only and no direction in space.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: A scalar quantity is fully described by its magnitude and unit. Since it has no spatial direction, scalar addition does not require head-to-tail construction or component resolution. For example, two time intervals can be added directly as numerical values with the same unit. The Reason states exactly why ordinary algebraic addition is suitable for scalars. This should not be extended carelessly to vectors, where direction affects both the magnitude and direction of the resultant.

question: Two bodies have velocities \(5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) east and \(5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) north. Their speeds are the same, but their velocities are not the same because:
opt_a: the unit \(\text{m s}^{-1}\) is different in the two cases
opt_b: east and north are different velocity directions
opt_c: speed must always be larger than velocity
opt_d: velocity has no magnitude in two-dimensional motion
explanation: The magnitude of each velocity is \(5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), so the two bodies have the same speed. Velocity, however, is a vector quantity. Two vectors are equal only when both their magnitudes and directions are the same. East and north are different directions, so the two velocities are different vectors. This is why equal speeds do not automatically mean equal velocities.

question:
Study the short description below.
A ball moves from point \(P\) to point \(Q\). One record gives the total length of the curved path followed by the ball. Another record gives the straight-line change from \(P\) to \(Q\).
The first and second records respectively describe:
explanation: The total length of the curved path is distance. Distance is scalar because it does not need a direction from the starting point to the ending point. The straight-line change from point \(P\) to point \(Q\) is displacement. Displacement is a vector because it has a magnitude and a direction from the initial point to the final point. A long curved path and its straight-line displacement can be very different, so path length should not be confused with change in position.

question:
Three statements about scalars and vectors are given.
I. A scalar may have a unit.
II. A vector must have a direction.
III. A negative sign always proves that a quantity is a vector.
The supported statements are:
explanation: A scalar quantity can have a unit; for example, time is measured in \(\text{s}\) and mass is measured in \(\text{kg}\). A vector quantity must have a direction along with magnitude. Statement III is not reliable because a negative sign may occur with scalar quantities in some contexts, such as temperature on the Celsius scale. A sign can also indicate direction for a component along a chosen axis, but that alone is not the definition of a vector. The real vector test is whether spatial direction is essential to the physical quantity.

question: A displacement is drawn as an arrow on paper. In this representation, the length of the arrow is used to show:
opt_c: the vector magnitude on the chosen scale
opt_d: the unit vector perpendicular to the displacement
explanation: A vector arrow represents both magnitude and direction. The direction is shown by the arrowhead, while the length represents the magnitude according to the chosen graphical scale. For example, \(1\,\text{cm}\) on paper may represent \(5\,\text{m}\) of displacement. The same physical vector may be drawn with a different length if a different scale is chosen. The arrow length on paper is not the actual time, mass, or a separate perpendicular vector.

question: In a vector arrow, the tail and head are important because:
opt_a: the tail shows the final point and the head shows the initial point
opt_b: the tail-to-head sense gives the direction of the vector
opt_c: the head always represents zero magnitude
opt_d: the tail is used only for scalar quantities
explanation: A vector arrow is read from its tail toward its head. The arrowhead shows the sense of the vector along the line on which it is drawn. If the head and tail are interchanged, the direction of the vector reverses. The magnitude may remain the same if the length is unchanged, but the vector itself changes because direction is part of a vector. This is why arrow orientation is as important as arrow length.

question: If a vector is denoted by \(\vec{A}\), then \(A=|\vec{A}|\) represents:
opt_a: a vector in the opposite direction
explanation: The symbol \(\vec{A}\) denotes the vector quantity, including both magnitude and direction. The notation \(A=|\vec{A}|\) denotes only the magnitude of that vector. Magnitude is a scalar and is never negative. Removing the arrow from the notation does not reverse the vector; it simply refers to its size. This distinction becomes important when vector equations are separated into magnitudes and directions.

question:
Use the scale information below.
On a vector diagram, the chosen scale is \(1\,\text{cm}=4\,\text{m}\). A displacement vector is drawn as an arrow of length \(3\,\text{cm}\) toward the east.
The physical displacement represented by the arrow is:
explanation:
\( \textbf{Scale given:} \) \(1\,\text{cm}\) on the diagram represents \(4\,\text{m}\) physically.
\( \textbf{Arrow length:} \) The drawn arrow has length \(3\,\text{cm}\).
\( \textbf{Magnitude represented:} \)
\[
3\,\text{cm}\times 4\,\text{m cm}^{-1}=12\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Direction:} \) The arrow points east, so the displacement direction is east.
\( \textbf{Why scale matters:} \) The drawn length \(3\,\text{cm}\) is not the actual displacement in metres; it must be converted using the diagram scale.
\( \textbf{Unit check:} \) The final physical displacement must be reported in \(\text{m}\), not in \(\text{cm}\), because the scale maps the drawing to real displacement.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The displacement represented is \(12\,\text{m}\) east.

question: Two arrows on a page represent vectors. Arrow P is \(4\,\text{cm}\) long and points north. Arrow Q is \(4\,\text{cm}\) long and points west. The two vectors are:
opt_a: equal because their drawn lengths are equal
opt_c: not equal because their directions differ
opt_d: not vectors because they are drawn on paper
explanation: Equal vectors must have both the same magnitude and the same direction. The equal lengths of arrows P and Q show equal magnitudes if the same scale is used. However, north and west are different directions. Since direction is a required part of a vector, the two arrows do not represent equal vectors. Equal magnitude alone gives equal size, not equal vector identity.

question: The notation pair \(\vec{A}\) and \(A\) is used in a solution. The most suitable interpretation is:
opt_a: \(\vec{A}\) is the magnitude and \(A\) is the direction
opt_b: \(\vec{A}\) is the vector and \(A\) is its magnitude
opt_c: both \(\vec{A}\) and \(A\) always represent zero vectors
opt_d: \(A\) is a vector only when it is written without units
explanation: The arrow over a symbol indicates that the quantity is being treated as a vector. Thus, \(\vec{A}\) carries direction along with magnitude. The symbol \(A\), when used as \(A=|\vec{A}|\), gives the magnitude of the vector. Magnitude is a scalar, so it does not point in any direction. This notation keeps vector equations and scalar magnitude calculations from being mixed carelessly.

question: A vector diagram is described as follows: an arrow starts at point \(P\), ends at point \(Q\), and is labelled \(\vec{d}\). The displacement represented by \(\vec{d}\) is:
opt_c: only the distance of point \(P\) from the origin
opt_d: the time taken to go from \(P\) to \(Q\)
explanation: A vector arrow is read from its tail to its head. Since the arrow starts at point \(P\) and ends at point \(Q\), the vector \(\vec{d}\) represents displacement from \(P\) to \(Q\). Reversing the direction would represent a different vector, usually written as \(-\vec{d}\). The label \(\vec{d}\) does not describe time; it describes a directed displacement. Direction is fixed by the order tail \(\rightarrow\) head, not merely by the two points being named.

question:
A row in a vector record is missing one entry.
VectorMagnitudeDirection
\(\vec{A}\)\(6\,\text{m}\)east
\(\vec{B}\)\(6\,\text{m}\)east
\(\vec{C}\)\(6\,\text{m}\)west
The relation supported by the table is:
explanation: Vectors \(\vec{A}\) and \(\vec{B}\) have the same magnitude, \(6\,\text{m}\), and the same direction, east. Therefore, they are equal vectors. Vector \(\vec{C}\) has the same magnitude but points west, which is opposite to east. Equal magnitude does not compensate for opposite direction in vector equality. The table shows that \(\vec{C}\) is not equal to either eastward vector, even though its length value matches theirs.

question: Two displacement arrows are drawn at different places on a map. Both arrows have length \(2\,\text{cm}\) on the same scale and both point northeast. The best conclusion is:
opt_a: they represent unequal vectors because their tails are at different points
explanation: Equal vectors must have the same magnitude and the same direction. The two arrows have the same drawn length on the same scale, so they represent the same magnitude. They also point northeast, so their directions match. A vector can be shifted parallel to itself without changing the vector it represents, as long as magnitude and direction remain unchanged. The location of the tail on the page does not by itself make two free vectors unequal.

question: A displacement vector \(\vec{A}\) points \(5\,\text{m}\) east. The vector \(-\vec{A}\) represents:
explanation: The negative of a vector has the same magnitude as the original vector but the opposite direction. Since \(\vec{A}\) is \(5\,\text{m}\) east, \(-\vec{A}\) must be \(5\,\text{m}\) west. The negative sign does not make the magnitude negative, because vector magnitude is always non-negative. It also does not double the vector. The sign changes the direction of the vector, not the size of its length.

question: A body starts from point \(P\), moves to point \(Q\), and then returns exactly to point \(P\). For the complete trip, the displacement vector is:
opt_a: equal to the total path length
opt_d: directed from \(Q\) to \(P\) with twice the path length
explanation: Displacement depends only on the initial and final positions. Here, the body starts at \(P\) and finally returns to \(P\). Since the initial and final positions are the same, the change in position is zero. The zero vector is written as \(\vec{0}\) and has zero magnitude. Even if the body has travelled a non-zero distance, its net displacement for the complete trip is not a directed vector from \(P\) to \(Q\).

question: The zero vector \(\vec{0}\) is different from an ordinary non-zero vector because it has:
opt_a: unit magnitude and no definite direction
opt_d: zero magnitude and no definite direction
explanation: The zero vector has magnitude \(0\). Since there is no length to point in any particular direction, its direction is not definite. It is useful in Physics when two equal and opposite vectors cancel or when initial and final positions are the same. A negative magnitude is not used for vectors; magnitude is always non-negative. Direction becomes meaningful only when the vector has a non-zero magnitude.

question:
Study the vector record below.
VectorMagnitudeDirection
\(\vec{P}\)\(8\,\text{m}\)south
\(\vec{Q}\)\(8\,\text{m}\)north
\(\vec{R}\)\(0\,\text{m}\)not definite
The relation best supported by the record is:
explanation: Vectors \(\vec{P}\) and \(\vec{Q}\) have the same magnitude, \(8\,\text{m}\), but opposite directions. A vector with the same magnitude and opposite direction is the negative of the original vector. Therefore, if \(\vec{P}\) points south, \(-\vec{P}\) points north with the same magnitude. The vector \(\vec{R}\) has zero magnitude, so it cannot be the negative of an \(8\,\text{m}\) vector. Equal vectors require the same direction, so \(\vec{P}\) and \(\vec{Q}\) are not equal.

question:
Three statements about equal, negative, and zero vectors are given.
I. Equal vectors must have the same magnitude and the same direction.
II. Negative vectors must have the same magnitude and opposite directions.
III. A zero vector has a definite direction along the positive \(x\)-axis.
The supported statements are:
explanation: Statement I is valid because vector equality requires both equal magnitude and identical direction. Statement II is also valid because the negative of a vector reverses direction while keeping the magnitude unchanged. Statement III is not valid because a zero vector has no definite direction. It is not automatically assigned to the positive \(x\)-axis or any other axis. This distinction prevents treating \(\vec{0}\) like a very small arrow pointing in some chosen direction.

question: Use the arrangement described below: an arrow from \(M\) to \(N\) represents \(\vec{d}\). Another arrow of the same length is drawn from \(N\) to \(M\). The second arrow represents:
explanation: The first arrow from \(M\) to \(N\) fixes the direction of \(\vec{d}\). The second arrow runs from \(N\) to \(M\), so its direction is exactly opposite. Since the two arrows have the same length, their magnitudes are the same. A vector with the same magnitude but the opposite direction is written as the negative of the original vector. It is not a zero vector, because its length is not zero.

question:
Assertion: The vectors \(4\,\text{m}\) east and \(4\,\text{m}\) west are not equal vectors.
Reason: Equal vectors must have the same magnitude, but their directions may be different.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: The assertion is true because \(4\,\text{m}\) east and \(4\,\text{m}\) west have opposite directions. Equal vectors require both equal magnitudes and the same direction. The reason is false because it says directions may be different for equal vectors. Equal magnitude alone is not enough for vector equality. The two given vectors are negatives of each other, not equal to each other.

question: Multiplying a vector \(\vec{A}\) by a positive real number \(k\) changes:
opt_c: magnitude becomes \(A/k\), with the same direction
explanation: When a vector is multiplied by a positive real number \(k\), the new vector is \(k\vec{A}\). Its magnitude becomes \(kA\), where \(A=|\vec{A}|\). Since \(k\gt0\), the direction remains the same as that of \(\vec{A}\). The vector does not become a scalar simply because it is multiplied by a scalar. Only the size is scaled when the multiplying number is positive.

question: If \(\vec{A}\) has magnitude \(6\,\text{m}\) toward north, then \(-2\vec{A}\) has:
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given vector:} \) \(\vec{A}\) has magnitude \(6\,\text{m}\) toward north.
\( \textbf{Multiplier:} \) The multiplier is \(-2\).
\( \textbf{Magnitude rule:} \) The magnitude of \(k\vec{A}\) is \(|k|A\).
\( \textbf{Magnitude calculation:} \)
\[
|-2|\times 6\,\text{m}=12\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Direction rule:} \) A negative multiplier reverses the direction of the vector.
\( \textbf{Direction change:} \) Opposite of north is south.
\( \textbf{Magnitude check:} \) The magnitude is not written as \(-12\,\text{m}\), because magnitudes are non-negative.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(-2\vec{A}\) has magnitude \(12\,\text{m}\) toward south.

question: The vector \(0\vec{A}\), where \(\vec{A}\) is a non-zero vector, is:
explanation: Multiplying any vector by \(0\) gives the zero vector. The magnitude becomes \(0\times A=0\). Since the resulting magnitude is zero, the resulting vector has no definite direction. It is not the same as \(\vec{A}\), because \(\vec{A}\) is given to be non-zero. It is also not \(-\vec{A}\), because \(-\vec{A}\) would have the same non-zero magnitude as \(\vec{A}\).

question:
A vector \(\vec{u}\) is multiplied by different real numbers. The row that gives the direction of the product most suitably is:
RowProductDirection compared with \(\vec{u}\)
P\(3\vec{u}\)same direction
Q\(-3\vec{u}\)opposite direction
R\(0\vec{u}\)same direction
S\(\frac{1}{2}\vec{u}\)same direction
The row that needs correction is:
explanation: A positive multiplier keeps the vector in the same direction, so rows P and S are suitable. A negative multiplier reverses the direction, so row Q is also suitable. For \(0\vec{u}\), the result is \(\vec{0}\), whose magnitude is zero. The zero vector has no definite direction, so it should not be described as having the same direction as \(\vec{u}\). Row R therefore needs correction because it assigns a definite direction to \(\vec{0}\).

question: A displacement vector \(\vec{s}\) represents \(10\,\text{m}\) west. A new vector is defined as \(\vec{p}=\frac{3}{2}\vec{s}\). The vector \(\vec{p}\) represents:
explanation:
\( \textbf{Original vector:} \) \(\vec{s}\) has magnitude \(10\,\text{m}\) and points west.
\( \textbf{Definition:} \) \(\vec{p}=\frac{3}{2}\vec{s}\).
\( \textbf{Multiplier sign:} \) The number \(\frac{3}{2}\) is positive.
\( \textbf{Direction effect:} \) A positive multiplier keeps the direction unchanged.
\( \textbf{Magnitude rule:} \)
\[
p=\left|\frac{3}{2}\right|s
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
p=\frac{3}{2}\times10\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
p=15\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(\vec{p}\) represents \(15\,\text{m}\) west.

question: A learner writes that if \(k=-1\), then \(k\vec{A}\) has “negative magnitude.” The better repair of this statement is:
explanation: For \(k=-1\), the product is \(-\vec{A}\). Its magnitude is \(|-1|A=A\), not \(-A\). The negative sign reverses the direction of the vector. It does not create a negative length, because vector magnitude is a non-negative scalar. The repaired statement must therefore keep the magnitude as \(A\) and place the effect of the negative sign on the direction.

question: For a non-zero vector \(\vec{A}\), compare \(2\vec{A}\) and \(-2\vec{A}\).
opt_a: They have equal magnitudes and the same direction
opt_b: They have unequal magnitudes and the same direction
opt_d: They have equal magnitudes and opposite directions
explanation: The magnitude of \(2\vec{A}\) is \(2A\). The magnitude of \(-2\vec{A}\) is also \(|-2|A=2A\). Thus, the magnitudes are equal. The positive multiplier \(2\) keeps the direction the same as \(\vec{A}\), while the negative multiplier \(-2\) reverses it. The two products have the same size but point in opposite directions.

question:
A graph description is given for scalar multiplication of a fixed non-zero vector \(\vec{A}\).
The horizontal axis shows the scalar multiplier \(k\). The vertical axis shows the magnitude of \(k\vec{A}\). The graph has a V-shape with its vertex at \(k=0\).
This graph shape is explained by the relation:
explanation: The magnitude of \(k\vec{A}\) depends on the absolute value of the multiplier \(k\). This gives the relation \(|k\vec{A}|=|k|A\). For positive \(k\), the magnitude increases as \(kA\). For negative \(k\), the magnitude still remains positive and increases as \((-k)A\) when \(k\) becomes more negative. At \(k=0\), the product is \(\vec{0}\), so the magnitude is \(0\). The V-shape appears because magnitude cannot become negative even when the scalar multiplier is negative.

question: Two displacement vectors are arranged head-to-tail: \(\vec{A}\) ends where \(\vec{B}\) begins. The resultant \(\vec{A}+\vec{B}\) is represented by the arrow drawn:
opt_a: from the head of \(\vec{A}\) to the tail of \(\vec{B}\)
opt_b: from the head of \(\vec{B}\) to the tail of \(\vec{A}\)
opt_c: from the tail of \(\vec{A}\) to the head of \(\vec{B}\)
opt_d: from the tail of \(\vec{B}\) to the head of \(\vec{A}\)
explanation: In the triangle law of vector addition, the second vector is placed so that its tail starts at the head of the first vector. The resultant is then drawn from the tail of the first vector to the head of the second vector. This single arrow represents the net effect of the two successive vectors. It is not drawn between the two touching points, because that would not represent the total change from start to finish. The construction follows the actual order of successive displacements while still giving the same vector sum for a different valid head-to-tail order.

question: Use the arrangement described below: an object moves from point \(P\) to point \(Q\), and then from point \(Q\) to point \(R\). The displacement from \(P\) to \(Q\) is \(\vec{a}\), and the displacement from \(Q\) to \(R\) is \(\vec{b}\). The net displacement is:
explanation: The two given displacements are already arranged head-to-tail. The first displacement carries the object from \(P\) to \(Q\), and the second carries it from \(Q\) to \(R\). The net displacement must connect the initial point \(P\) directly to the final point \(R\). This is the geometric meaning of \(\vec{a}+\vec{b}\). The distance \(PQ+QR\) is the total path length, while the vector sum is a directed change from the first position to the last position.

question: A walker goes \(30\,\text{m}\) east and then \(40\,\text{m}\) north. The triangle-law construction of the resultant displacement requires the second arrow to be drawn:
opt_a: from the starting point of the eastward arrow
opt_b: from a separate origin unrelated to the first arrow
opt_d: from the head of the eastward arrow
explanation: In a head-to-tail construction, each next vector begins where the previous vector ends. The eastward displacement is drawn first, and the northward displacement must start from the head of that eastward arrow. The resultant then joins the original starting point to the final head of the northward arrow. Drawing both arrows from the same starting point would no longer be the triangle-law arrangement, though it is used in the parallelogram law. The construction must preserve both the magnitude and direction of each displacement.

question: Two vectors \(\vec{A}\) and \(\vec{B}\) are added graphically by the triangle law. A common wrong diagram draws the resultant from the head of \(\vec{A}\) back to the tail of \(\vec{B}\). The error in this diagram is that:
opt_b: it makes the magnitude of \(\vec{B}\) zero
opt_c: it converts both vectors into scalars
opt_d: it proves that vector addition is impossible
explanation: The resultant in the triangle law must be drawn from the first tail to the last head. If the arrow is drawn from the last head back toward the first tail, it points in the opposite direction to the required resultant. The magnitude may be the same as the correct resultant in such a reversed drawing, but the direction is wrong. Since vector direction matters, the reversed arrow represents the negative of the required resultant. A graphical vector construction must fix both the endpoints and the arrow sense.

question: The statement \(\vec{A}+\vec{B}=\vec{B}+\vec{A}\) for two vectors means that:
opt_a: the vectors must have equal magnitudes
opt_b: order changes the path, not the resultant
opt_c: the two vectors must point in the same direction
opt_d: the resultant is always a zero vector
explanation: Vector addition is commutative, so changing the order of adding two vectors does not change the final resultant. In a head-to-tail diagram, \(\vec{A}\) may be followed by \(\vec{B}\), or \(\vec{B}\) may be followed by \(\vec{A}\). The intermediate path on the diagram can look different, but the starting point and final point of the resultant are equivalent. This does not require the vectors to have equal magnitudes or the same direction. Order independence applies to the vector sum, not to the physical route followed in every real situation.

The row that describes the resultant incorrectly is:
explanation: Row P only states that \(\vec{u}\) is drawn first, so it is acceptable. Row Q correctly places the tail of \(\vec{v}\) at the head of \(\vec{u}\), which is the head-to-tail arrangement. Row R correctly states the resultant as the arrow from the tail of the first vector to the head of the second vector. Row S wrongly places the resultant between the touching points of the two vectors. The touching point is only the connection point for construction, not the start or end of the total displacement.

question: A map uses the scale \(1\,\text{cm}=10\,\text{m}\). A head-to-tail displacement diagram shows \(\vec{A}\) as \(3\,\text{cm}\) east, followed by \(\vec{B}\) as \(4\,\text{cm}\) north. The resultant arrow from the starting point to the final point measures \(5\,\text{cm}\) on the map. The magnitude of the resultant displacement is:
explanation:
\( \textbf{Scale:} \) \(1\,\text{cm}=10\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Measured resultant length:} \) The resultant arrow on the map is \(5\,\text{cm}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Physical magnitude of the resultant displacement.
\( \textbf{Scale conversion:} \)
\[
5\,\text{cm}\times10\,\text{m cm}^{-1}=50\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Why the resultant arrow is used:} \) In the triangle law, the resultant is the arrow from the first tail to the last head.
\( \textbf{Path-length contrast:} \) The separate path arrows have lengths \(3\,\text{cm}\) and \(4\,\text{cm}\), but the resultant is not found by adding these map lengths when the directions differ.
\( \textbf{Unit check:} \) The final answer must be in \(\text{m}\), because the question asks for physical displacement.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The magnitude of the resultant displacement is \(50\,\text{m}\).

question:
Assertion: In the triangle law, \(\vec{A}+\vec{B}\) is represented by the third side of the triangle taken in a definite direction.
Reason: The resultant runs from the tail of the first vector to the head of the second vector in a head-to-tail arrangement.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: The triangle law uses two vectors placed head-to-tail. The resultant is the third side of the triangle, but its direction must be taken from the start of the first vector to the end of the second vector. Without this direction, the third side could be read oppositely and would represent the negative of the desired resultant. The Reason gives the construction rule that fixes the direction of the third side. The phrase “third side” alone is incomplete unless the arrow sense is also specified.

question: A resultant vector is obtained by adding two vectors using the triangle law. If both original vectors are shifted parallel to themselves without changing their lengths or directions, the resultant:
opt_a: changes because the vectors start at new points
opt_b: the same resultant vector is obtained
explanation: A vector is determined by its magnitude and direction, not by the particular location where it is drawn on a page. In a triangle-law construction, vectors may be shifted parallel to themselves to place them head-to-tail. This shifting does not change the vectors being added. If the lengths and directions are preserved, the resulting vector sum is unchanged. The physical meaning of displacement addition depends on directed changes, not on the drawing’s absolute position on the sheet.

question: In the parallelogram law of vector addition, two vectors to be added are first drawn:
opt_c: with one vector starting at the head of the other only
opt_d: as two sides that never meet
explanation: The parallelogram law starts by drawing the two vectors from the same initial point. These two vectors form two adjacent sides of a parallelogram. After completing the parallelogram, the diagonal from the common tail gives the resultant. This differs from the triangle law, where the second vector is placed at the head of the first vector. Both methods give the same vector sum when the construction is done with correct magnitudes and directions.

question: Use the arrangement described below: two arrows \(\vec{p}\) and \(\vec{q}\) are drawn from the same point \(O\). A parallelogram is completed using these arrows as adjacent sides. The resultant \(\vec{p}+\vec{q}\) is:
opt_a: the diagonal joining the two heads of \(\vec{p}\) and \(\vec{q}\)
opt_b: the side opposite to \(\vec{p}\) taken alone
opt_c: the side opposite to \(\vec{q}\) taken alone
opt_d: the diagonal from \(O\) to the opposite corner
explanation: In the parallelogram law, the two vectors are drawn from a common tail \(O\). The parallelogram is then completed by drawing sides parallel to the two vectors. The resultant is the diagonal that starts from the common tail and reaches the opposite corner. The other diagonal joins the heads of the two vectors and does not represent \(\vec{p}+\vec{q}\). The starting point of the resultant is important because it represents the combined effect beginning from the same point.

question: The triangle law and parallelogram law give the same resultant for two vectors because:
opt_a: both ignore the directions of the vectors
opt_b: they represent the same vector sum in different graphical forms
opt_c: both work only when the two vectors have equal magnitudes
opt_d: both always make the resultant equal to the larger vector
explanation: The triangle law places the second vector at the head of the first and draws the resultant from the first tail to the last head. The parallelogram law draws both vectors from the same tail and uses the diagonal through the completed parallelogram. The side of the parallelogram parallel to one vector effectively reproduces the head-to-tail construction. Thus, the two methods are graphically different but physically equivalent. Neither method ignores direction, because the direction of each side and the resultant is essential.

question: A diagram has two vectors \(\vec{A}\) and \(\vec{B}\) drawn from the same point. One diagonal of the completed parallelogram starts from the common tail, while the other diagonal joins the two arrowheads. For vector addition, the required diagonal is:
opt_a: the one joining the two arrowheads
opt_b: the one starting from the common tail
opt_c: either diagonal, because diagonals are always equal
opt_d: neither diagonal, because vector addition cannot be graphical
explanation: The diagonal used in the parallelogram law must begin at the common tail of the two vectors. This diagonal points toward the opposite corner of the parallelogram and represents \(\vec{A}+\vec{B}\). The diagonal joining the two arrowheads has a different direction and a different physical meaning. It is related to the difference between the vectors, not their sum. Selecting the correct diagonal is a direction-sensitive part of the construction.

Row S uses the other diagonal, which joins the two arrowheads. That diagonal is not the resultant of \(\vec{A}\) and \(\vec{B}\). The resultant must start from the common starting point because it represents the combined effect of both vectors taken from that point.

question: A force of graphical length \(4\,\text{cm}\) is drawn toward east and another of graphical length \(4\,\text{cm}\) is drawn toward north from the same point. Without calculating a numerical angle, the parallelogram resultant must point:
explanation: The parallelogram resultant is the diagonal drawn from the common tail. Since one vector points east and the other points north, the diagonal must lie between these two directions. Equal magnitudes make the diagonal symmetrically placed between east and north, but the important idea here is that the resultant lies inside the angle between the two vectors. It cannot point opposite to both vectors because both contributions have eastward or northward tendencies. The direction of a resultant reflects the combined directional effects of the vectors being added.

question: A vector diagram shows two unequal vectors drawn from a common tail, and the completed parallelogram is slanted. The diagonal from the common tail is closer in direction to the longer vector. This happens because:
opt_a: the longer vector contributes more to the resultant direction
opt_b: the shorter vector is ignored completely
opt_c: the parallelogram law works only for unequal vectors
opt_d: the resultant must always be perpendicular to the longer vector
explanation: The resultant of two vectors depends on both their magnitudes and their directions. If one vector is longer, it has a stronger influence on the direction of the diagonal from the common tail. The shorter vector still affects the resultant, so it is not ignored. The parallelogram law works for equal as well as unequal vectors. A resultant is not required to be perpendicular to either vector; its direction is fixed by the diagonal of the completed parallelogram.

question: Several displacement vectors are placed one after another so that the head of each vector touches the tail of the next vector. The resultant in the polygon law is drawn:
opt_a: from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last vector
opt_b: from the head of the first vector to the tail of the last vector
opt_c: from the head of the last vector to the tail of the first vector
opt_d: only along the longest side of the polygon
explanation: The polygon law extends the head-to-tail idea from two vectors to several vectors. Each vector is drawn with its magnitude and direction unchanged, beginning at the head of the previous vector. After all vectors are placed, the resultant connects the starting point of the first vector to the ending point of the last vector. The resultant is therefore a single directed arrow representing the total change. It is not chosen by looking for the longest side, because vector addition depends on the complete head-to-tail arrangement.

question: Use the route described below: a person walks from point \(P\) to point \(Q\), then from \(Q\) to point \(R\), and finally from \(R\) to point \(S\). The three displacements are \(\vec{a}\), \(\vec{b}\), and \(\vec{c}\) respectively. The vector \(\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}\) is represented by:
opt_d: the directed displacement from \(Q\) to \(R\) only
explanation: The displacements are already arranged in a head-to-tail chain. The first begins at \(P\), the second begins where the first ends, and the third begins where the second ends. The resultant of all three displacements must connect the original starting point \(P\) to the final point \(S\). This is the polygon-law meaning of \(\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}\). The path length adds lengths without direction, while the vector sum gives the single net displacement.

question: A closed vector polygon is formed when four non-zero vectors are arranged head-to-tail and the head of the fourth vector reaches the tail of the first. The resultant of the four vectors is:
opt_a: the longest vector in the polygon
opt_b: the shortest vector in the polygon
opt_d: the sum of the magnitudes of all four vectors
explanation: In a closed polygon, the final point coincides with the initial point. The resultant vector is drawn from the initial point of the first vector to the final point of the last vector. Since these two points are the same, the resultant has zero magnitude. This gives the zero vector \(\vec{0}\). The individual vectors may all be non-zero, but their combined directed effect cancels over the full closed path.

question: A drone flies \(6\,\text{m}\) east, then \(8\,\text{m}\) north, and finally \(6\,\text{m}\) west. The magnitude and direction of its net displacement are:
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given route:} \) \(6\,\text{m}\) east, \(8\,\text{m}\) north, and \(6\,\text{m}\) west.
\( \textbf{Horizontal effects:} \) The \(6\,\text{m}\) east displacement and \(6\,\text{m}\) west displacement are equal and opposite.
\( \textbf{Horizontal resultant:} \)
\[
6\,\text{m east}+6\,\text{m west}=0
\]
\( \textbf{Vertical effect:} \) The only remaining displacement is \(8\,\text{m}\) north.
\( \textbf{Polygon-law view:} \) The head-to-tail path begins at the starting point and ends \(8\,\text{m}\) north of it.
\( \textbf{Distance contrast:} \) The total distance travelled is \(20\,\text{m}\), but displacement depends only on the initial and final positions.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The net displacement is \(8\,\text{m}\) north.

Row R is also valid because returning to the starting point means net displacement is zero. Row S is not generally true because the arithmetic sum of magnitudes is obtained only when all vectors act in the same direction. In a polygon arrangement, different directions can partly or fully cancel one another, so vector addition cannot be replaced by ordinary length addition.

question: Three vectors \(\vec{p}\), \(\vec{q}\), and \(\vec{r}\) are added by placing them head-to-tail. If their order is changed but each vector keeps the same magnitude and direction, the final resultant:
opt_a: must change because the path shape changes
opt_c: becomes the zero vector every time
opt_d: becomes equal to the first vector in the new order
explanation: Vector addition is independent of the order of addition. Changing the order of \(\vec{p}\), \(\vec{q}\), and \(\vec{r}\) may change the intermediate shape of the drawn polygon. However, the final vector sum remains unchanged if all three vectors keep their original magnitudes and directions. This is a graphical expression of the commutative and associative properties of vector addition. The visible route on the paper may differ, but the resultant vector represents the same total directed effect.

question: A vector polygon has sides representing \(\vec{A}\), \(\vec{B}\), and \(\vec{C}\) in head-to-tail order. The final point lies \(5\,\text{cm}\) east of the starting point on a diagram with scale \(1\,\text{cm}=2\,\text{m}\). The magnitude of \(\vec{A}+\vec{B}+\vec{C}\) is:
explanation:
\( \textbf{Diagram scale:} \) \(1\,\text{cm}=2\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Resultant arrow on diagram:} \) The final point is \(5\,\text{cm}\) east of the starting point.
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Magnitude of \(\vec{A}+\vec{B}+\vec{C}\).
\( \textbf{Scale conversion:} \)
\[
5\,\text{cm}\times2\,\text{m cm}^{-1}=10\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Direction note:} \) The resultant points east, but the question asks only for magnitude.
\( \textbf{Polygon-law meaning:} \) The resultant is measured from the first tail to the last head, not by adding all side lengths.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The magnitude of the resultant is \(10\,\text{m}\).

question: The relation \((\vec{A}+\vec{B})+\vec{C}=\vec{A}+(\vec{B}+\vec{C})\) expresses:
opt_a: the definition of a zero vector
opt_c: the multiplication of a vector by a scalar
explanation: The given relation says that the grouping of three vectors during addition does not change the final resultant. This is called the associative property of vector addition. It allows \(\vec{A}\) and \(\vec{B}\) to be added first, or \(\vec{B}\) and \(\vec{C}\) to be added first, without changing the final sum. The property does not mean that direction can be ignored; each vector must still be added with its own direction. Grouping may change the intermediate step, but not the final resultant.

question: In a head-to-tail drawing, \(\vec{A}+\vec{B}\) and \(\vec{B}+\vec{A}\) form different-looking intermediate paths. The reason their resultants are still equal is that:
opt_b: direction is not used in vector diagrams
explanation: The commutative property of vector addition states that \(\vec{A}+\vec{B}=\vec{B}+\vec{A}\). Graphically, the two head-to-tail arrangements may trace different sides of a parallelogram. Even so, the diagonal representing the resultant is the same in magnitude and direction. This property is about the final vector sum, not about the drawn route having the same shape. Direction remains essential for each vector, even though the order of addition may be changed.

question:
Three statements about vector addition are listed.
I. \(\vec{A}+\vec{B}=\vec{B}+\vec{A}\).
II. \((\vec{A}+\vec{B})+\vec{C}=\vec{A}+(\vec{B}+\vec{C})\).
III. Vector addition allows directions to be ignored if magnitudes are known.
The supported statements are:
explanation: Statement I gives the commutative property of vector addition. Statement II gives the associative property of vector addition. Both are valid for vectors when the vectors are added with their proper magnitudes and directions. Statement III is not valid because direction is essential in vector addition. These algebraic-looking properties do not convert vector addition into ordinary addition of magnitudes.

question: A solution first combines \(\vec{P}\) and \(\vec{Q}\), then adds \(\vec{R}\). Another solution first combines \(\vec{Q}\) and \(\vec{R}\), then adds \(\vec{P}\). If all vectors are unchanged, the two final resultants are:
opt_a: unequal because grouping is always forbidden
opt_b: zero because three vectors are involved
opt_d: equal only if all three vectors point north
explanation: Associativity means that the grouping used during vector addition does not change the final vector sum. The first solution evaluates \((\vec{P}+\vec{Q})+\vec{R}\). The second solution evaluates \(\vec{P}+(\vec{Q}+\vec{R})\). These expressions have the same resultant as long as the original vectors are the same. The property is useful in multi-vector addition because it allows convenient grouping without changing the final directed result.

question: Subtracting a vector \(\vec{B}\) from another vector \(\vec{A}\) is best understood as:
explanation: Vector subtraction is defined through vector addition. The expression \(\vec{A}-\vec{B}\) means \(\vec{A}+(-\vec{B})\). To construct it graphically, \(\vec{B}\) is reversed to obtain \(-\vec{B}\), and then this reversed vector is added to \(\vec{A}\). The magnitude of \(\vec{B}\) alone is not enough because the direction of \(\vec{B}\) must be handled. Subtraction changes the direction of the vector being subtracted, not the direction of every vector in the expression.

question: A displacement vector \(\vec{A}\) is \(7\,\text{m}\) east and \(\vec{B}\) is \(3\,\text{m}\) east. The vector \(\vec{A}-\vec{B}\) is:
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given vectors:} \) \(\vec{A}=7\,\text{m}\) east and \(\vec{B}=3\,\text{m}\) east.
\( \textbf{Subtraction rule:} \)
\[
\vec{A}-\vec{B}=\vec{A}+(-\vec{B})
\]
\( \textbf{Negative of \(\vec{B}\):} \) Since \(\vec{B}\) is \(3\,\text{m}\) east, \(-\vec{B}\) is \(3\,\text{m}\) west.
\( \textbf{Combination:} \) \(7\,\text{m}\) east combined with \(3\,\text{m}\) west leaves \(4\,\text{m}\) east.
\( \textbf{Magnitude check:} \) The vectors lie along the same line, so the smaller opposite effect is subtracted from the larger one.
\( \textbf{Direction check:} \) The larger original eastward effect decides the final direction.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(\vec{A}-\vec{B}=4\,\text{m}\) east.

question: Use the arrangement described below: two position vectors \(\vec{r}_1\) and \(\vec{r}_2\) are drawn from the same origin to points \(P\) and \(Q\) respectively. The vector \(\vec{r}_2-\vec{r}_1\) represents:
opt_c: the sum of distances from the origin to \(P\) and \(Q\)
opt_d: the zero vector for all positions of \(P\) and \(Q\)
explanation: The position vector \(\vec{r}_1\) locates point \(P\) from the origin, and \(\vec{r}_2\) locates point \(Q\) from the same origin. The difference \(\vec{r}_2-\vec{r}_1\) gives the change from the first position to the second position. Geometrically, this is the vector that starts at \(P\) and ends at \(Q\). The common origin helps define both position vectors, but the difference itself connects the two points. Reversing the order to \(\vec{r}_1-\vec{r}_2\) would reverse the direction of the displacement.

explanation: Row P correctly uses the definition \(\vec{A}-\vec{B}=\vec{A}+(-\vec{B})\). Row Q applies the same idea with the order reversed. question: The vectors \(\vec{A}\) and \(\vec{B}\) have equal magnitudes but opposite directions. The value of \(\vec{A}-\vec{B}\) is:
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given relation:} \) \(\vec{B}\) has the same magnitude as \(\vec{A}\) but the opposite direction.

\]
\( \textbf{Required expression:} \)
\[
\vec{A}-\vec{B}
\]

\vec{A}-\vec{B}=\vec{A}-(-\vec{A})
\]
\( \textbf{Simplify signs:} \)

question: Two vectors of magnitudes \(A\) and \(B\) make an angle \(\theta\) with each other. The magnitude of their resultant is given by:
explanation: When two vectors are added at an angle \(\theta\), their resultant depends on both magnitudes and the included angle. The formula comes from applying the cosine rule to the vector triangle or parallelogram. The term \(2AB\cos\theta\) accounts for how much the two vectors support or oppose each other in direction. The square root is needed because \(A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta\) gives \(R^2\), not \(R\). The angle \(\theta\) must be the angle between the two vectors when their tails are placed together.

question: The expression \(2AB\cos\theta\) in the resultant formula mainly represents:
opt_a: the effect of time on vector addition
opt_b: the angle-dependent part of the resultant
opt_d: the condition that both vectors must be zero
explanation: The resultant formula is \(R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta}\). The terms \(A^2\) and \(B^2\) represent the individual magnitudes in the cosine-rule structure. The cross term \(2AB\cos\theta\) changes as the angle between the vectors changes. If the angle is small, \(\cos\theta\) is positive and the vectors support each other more strongly. If the angle is large, \(\cos\theta\) may become negative and the resultant is reduced. This term is the mathematical place where direction enters the magnitude calculation.

question: Two vectors of magnitudes \(6\,\text{N}\) and \(8\,\text{N}\) act at an angle of \(60^\circ\). The magnitude of their resultant is:
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(A=6\,\text{N}\), \(B=8\,\text{N}\), and \(\theta=60^\circ\).
\( \textbf{Required:} \) Magnitude \(R\) of the resultant.

\[

\]
\( \textbf{Why it applies:} \) Two vectors of known magnitudes are acting with a known included angle.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)

\]

\[

\]

\]

\]

\[

\]

\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The resultant magnitude is approximately \(12.2\,\text{N}\).

question: A student uses \(R=A+B\) for two non-parallel vectors of magnitudes \(A\) and \(B\). The main error is that:
opt_a: \(R=A+B\) is valid only when the vectors are perpendicular
opt_b: \(R=A+B\) ignores the angle between the vectors

opt_d: \(R=A+B\) always gives the minimum possible resultant
explanation: The magnitude of the sum of two vectors generally depends on the angle between them. The complete relation is \(R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta}\). The simple sum \(A+B\) occurs only when the vectors act in the same direction, so \(\theta=0^\circ\). For non-parallel vectors, some part of one vector is not along the direction of the other. Adding magnitudes directly would overestimate the resultant unless the two vectors point exactly the same way.

question: Two equal vectors of magnitude \(10\,\text{m}\) make an angle of \(120^\circ\) with each other. Their resultant magnitude is:
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(A=10\,\text{m}\), \(B=10\,\text{m}\), and \(\theta=120^\circ\).
\( \textbf{Required:} \) Resultant magnitude \(R\).

\[
R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
R=\sqrt{10^2+10^2+2(10)(10)\cos120^\circ}
\]
\( \textbf{Angle value:} \)
\[
\cos120^\circ=-\frac{1}{2}
\]
\( \textbf{Cross term:} \)
\[
2(10)(10)\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=-100
\]
\( \textbf{Inside the square root:} \)
\[
R=\sqrt{100+100-100}
\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[
R=\sqrt{100}=10\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Physical reading:} \) The vectors are not opposite, so the resultant is not zero, but the obtuse angle reduces it strongly.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The resultant magnitude is \(10\,\text{m}\).

question: For two vectors at angle \(\theta\), the direction of the resultant relative to \(\vec{A}\) is often written as:
explanation: The angle \(\alpha\) is measured from \(\vec{A}\) toward the resultant. The component of \(\vec{B}\) perpendicular to \(\vec{A}\) is \(B\sin\theta\). The component along \(\vec{A}\) combines with \(\vec{A}\) itself to give \(A+B\cos\theta\). Therefore, \(\tan\alpha\) is the perpendicular part divided by the along-\(\vec{A}\) part. This relation assumes that \(\theta\) is the angle from \(\vec{A}\) to \(\vec{B}\), so the reference direction must be chosen consistently.

question: A pair of vectors has \(A=12\,\text{N}\), \(B=5\,\text{N}\), and \(\theta=90^\circ\). The angle \(\alpha\) made by the resultant with \(\vec{A}\) satisfies:
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(A=12\,\text{N}\), \(B=5\,\text{N}\), and \(\theta=90^\circ\).
\( \textbf{Required:} \) Direction relation for the resultant with respect to \(\vec{A}\).
\( \textbf{Direction formula:} \)
\[
\tan\alpha=\frac{B\sin\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}
\]
\( \textbf{Angle values:} \)
\[
\sin90^\circ=1,\qquad \cos90^\circ=0
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\tan\alpha=\frac{5(1)}{12+5(0)}
\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[
\tan\alpha=\frac{5}{12}
\]
\( \textbf{Direction meaning:} \) The resultant tilts away from \(\vec{A}\) toward \(\vec{B}\), but less than \(45^\circ\) because \(A\) is larger than \(B\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(\tan\alpha=\frac{5}{12}\).

question: Given \(A=9\,\text{N}\), \(B=7\,\text{N}\), and resultant magnitude \(R=14\,\text{N}\), the value of \(\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between the two vectors, is:
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(A=9\,\text{N}\), \(B=7\,\text{N}\), and \(R=14\,\text{N}\).
\( \textbf{Required:} \) \(\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the included angle.
\( \textbf{Resultant relation:} \)
\[
R^2=A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta
\]
\( \textbf{Rearrange:} \)
\[
\cos\theta=\frac{R^2-A^2-B^2}{2AB}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\cos\theta=\frac{14^2-9^2-7^2}{2(9)(7)}
\]
\( \textbf{Squares:} \)
\[
14^2=196,\qquad 9^2=81,\qquad 7^2=49
\]
\( \textbf{Numerator:} \)
\[
196-81-49=66
\]
\( \textbf{Denominator:} \)
\[
2(9)(7)=126
\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[
\cos\theta=\frac{66}{126}=\frac{11}{21}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The value of \(\cos\theta\) is \(\frac{11}{21}\).

question: A pair of vectors has fixed magnitudes \(A\) and \(B\). As the angle \(\theta\) between them is increased from \(0^\circ\) to \(180^\circ\), the magnitude of the resultant:
opt_c: remains equal to \(A+B\) for all angles
opt_d: remains equal to \(\sqrt{A^2+B^2}\) for all angles
explanation: The resultant magnitude is \(R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta}\). As \(\theta\) increases from \(0^\circ\) to \(180^\circ\), \(\cos\theta\) decreases from \(1\) to \(-1\). Therefore, the term \(2AB\cos\theta\) decreases from its maximum positive value to its most negative value. At \(\theta=0^\circ\), the vectors are in the same direction and \(R=A+B\). At \(\theta=180^\circ\), the vectors are opposite and \(R=|A-B|\). The angle controls how much the two vectors support or cancel each other.

question:

Reason: In the formula \(R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta}\), the term \(\cos\theta\) has its maximum value at \(\theta=0^\circ\).
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion

opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: The assertion is true because two vectors give their largest resultant when they act in the same direction. In that case, the angle between them is \(0^\circ\), and their magnitudes add directly. The reason is also true because \(\cos0^\circ=1\), which is the maximum possible value of \(\cos\theta\) in this context. This makes the term \(2AB\cos\theta\) as large as possible. Since \(A\) and \(B\) are fixed, maximizing this term maximizes \(R^2\) and therefore \(R\). The reason gives the mathematical explanation behind the maximum-resultant condition.

question: In deriving the resultant formula for two vectors \(\vec{A}\) and \(\vec{B}\), the angle between the two vectors is \(\theta\), but the angle used inside the triangle formed by head-to-tail placement becomes \(180^\circ-\theta\). This leads to the \(+2AB\cos\theta\) term because:
opt_a: \(\cos(180^\circ-\theta)=-\cos\theta\), so the minus sign changes it to plus
opt_b: \(\sin(180^\circ-\theta)=\sin\theta\), so the cosine term becomes a sine term
opt_c: \(\cos(180^\circ-\theta)=\cos\theta\), so the cross term keeps the same sign
opt_d: \(180^\circ-\theta\) is replaced by \(0^\circ\), so the cross term becomes maximum
explanation: In the head-to-tail triangle, the side representing the resultant is found using the cosine rule. The angle inside the triangle opposite the resultant is \(180^\circ-\theta\), not \(\theta\) itself. The cosine rule contains a term of the form \(-2AB\cos(180^\circ-\theta)\). Since \(\cos(180^\circ-\theta)=-\cos\theta\), the two negative signs combine to give \(+2AB\cos\theta\). This is why the final formula becomes \(R^2=A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta\). The sign of the cross term is tied to the geometry of the vector triangle, not inserted arbitrarily.

question: For two vectors of magnitudes \(12\,\text{N}\) and \(5\,\text{N}\), the possible values of the resultant magnitude must lie in the range:

question: The direction formula \(\tan\alpha=\frac{B\sin\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}\) gives \(\alpha\) measured:
explanation: In the usual direction formula, \(\vec{A}\) is taken as the reference direction. The component of \(\vec{B}\) along \(\vec{A}\) is \(B\cos\theta\), so the total component along \(\vec{A}\) is \(A+B\cos\theta\). The component of \(\vec{B}\) perpendicular to \(\vec{A}\) is \(B\sin\theta\). The tangent of the angle made by the resultant with \(\vec{A}\) is therefore perpendicular component divided by parallel component. Using the formula without knowing the reference direction can give a direction angle measured from the wrong vector.

question: For \(A=5\,\text{N}\), \(B=10\,\text{N}\), and \(\theta=120^\circ\), the resultant makes what angle \(\alpha\) with \(\vec{A}\)?
explanation:

\]

\]

\[

\]

\]

\[
B\sin\theta=10\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)=5\sqrt{3}
\]
\( \textbf{Direction meaning:} \) The parallel component along \(\vec{A}\) is zero, while the perpendicular component is non-zero.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The resultant is perpendicular to \(\vec{A}\), so \(\alpha=90^\circ\).

question: Two vectors of magnitudes \(10\,\text{N}\) and \(6\,\text{N}\) make an angle of \(60^\circ\). The resultant magnitude and the value of \(\tan\alpha\), where \(\alpha\) is measured from the \(10\,\text{N}\) vector, are:
explanation:

\( \textbf{Required:} \) Resultant magnitude \(R\) and direction relation \(\tan\alpha\).
\( \textbf{Magnitude formula:} \)
\[
R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitute for \(R\):} \)
\[
R=\sqrt{10^2+6^2+2(10)(6)\cos60^\circ}
\]
\( \textbf{Use \(\cos60^\circ=\frac{1}{2}\):} \)
\[
R=\sqrt{100+36+120\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}
\]
\( \textbf{Simplify:} \)
\[
R=\sqrt{100+36+60}=\sqrt{196}=14\,\text{N}
\]
\( \textbf{Direction formula:} \)
\[
\tan\alpha=\frac{B\sin\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitute angle values:} \)
\[
\tan\alpha=\frac{6\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)}{10+6\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}
\]
\( \textbf{Simplify numerator and denominator:} \)
\[
\tan\alpha=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{13}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The resultant is \(14\,\text{N}\), and \(\tan\alpha=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{13}\).
